This guide assumes you have already read [*The Spell Writing Guide*](https://www.gorillaofdestiny.com/books-and-compendiums) by The Gorilla of Destiny. Its binary-pattern and chord-based approach is the conceptual foundation for Sigil. Here, we follow a spell from its selected mechanics and identifying source/variant ID through the current calculations and into a rendered sigil.

**Encoded information is not the same as visible strokes.** A chord can be bent, an orbit can be hidden, and a fingerprint mark can be restyled without changing what was calculated. Understanding that distinction makes the three layers easier to follow.

The order matters: preprocessing chooses *what* to represent; legibility determines *where* to represent it; shared encoding turns choices into bits; layer calculations turn bits into data; drawing makes that data visible.

## 1. Why these attributes and these three layers?

There are two separate design decisions: **which mechanical attributes to include**, and **how to distribute their information across the image**.

**First, select a useful mechanical vocabulary.** Historical preprocessing compared how well combinations of categorical attributes distinguished spells in a Pathfinder 2e catalogue. The historical experiment described in the revision brief used **1,403 records**, required **seven core mechanics**, and imposed a maximum of **nine categorical attributes**. It compared the added distinctiveness offered by candidate fields under those constraints. The current catalogue described by the supplied calculation guide contains **1,400 records**; the historical counts should not be mistaken for measurements on that newer catalogue. The resulting nine-attribute vocabulary is a practical, data-informed choice **within a specified limit**, not proof that nine is an unconstrained mathematical optimum.

**Second, make that vocabulary legible.** Encoding nine attributes as nine separate chord families would create a crowded web of crossing connections. Sigil therefore keeps a Guide-inspired first layer of **five chord families on eleven vertices** and assigns the **other four mechanical attributes** to circular **orbits** centered on individual vertices. These circles carry information locally, without creating more vertex-to-vertex crossings, and are intended to be easier to recognize. This five/four allocation is a visual design decision, **not** a conclusion established by the historical attribute-selection experiment.

Even nine mechanics cannot identify every spell uniquely: two catalogue records can have the same mechanical categories. A separate, third layer therefore encodes an assigned **spell fingerprint** from the source/variant ID, independently of those categories.

| Layer | Encoded input | Representation |
|---|---|---|
| **1 - Vertices** | Rank, Tradition, Range, Duration, Primary Trait | Five chord families on eleven vertices |
| **2 — Orbits** | Damage, Area, Casting time, Casting traits | One weighted circular arc or full circle per active vertex |
| **3 — Spell fingerprint** | Source/variant ID, **not another mechanical attribute** | Ordered binary markers |

## 2. Shared encoding: from a category to bits

Layers 1 and 2 begin with the **same conversion**, before either chords or orbits are calculated:

**Chosen category → index in that attribute's ordered options → fixed binary pattern → consistent rotation → active vertices.**

Each attribute has an ordered list of allowed category values. For a non-`none` selection, Sigil finds its **zero-based index** in that list (excluding a `none` sentinel, where one exists), selects the corresponding dictionary pattern, and applies a deterministic left rotation. The resulting word contains **eleven bits**: the leftmost represents vertex `0`, the rightmost vertex `10`. A `0` means inactive; a `1` means active. Where `none` applies, it bypasses the dictionary and becomes the all-zero word, `00000000000`.

The dictionary is organized around **binary necklaces**. Imagine rotating a string of bits around a circle: patterns that differ only because they start at different points belong to the same rotation family. Sigil keeps a consistent representative for each family rather than treating every rotation as a new pattern. The current eleven-bit dictionary contains **186 nonconstant necklaces**, arranged in a fixed order. A consistent rotation of the selected representative then determines which numbered vertices are active.

The **order of options** is part of the calculation, not just an interface detail. Reproducing or reversing the result requires the same option lists and the same ordered dictionary; this matters especially for Range options appended from a loaded catalogue. No chord, orbit, or fingerprint mark has yet been drawn at this stage.

## 3. Layer 1 - Vertices

The first layer uses the shared active vertices to create **logical connections between pairs of vertices**. Five primary mechanical attributes need five distinguishable connection rules. The shipped scheme uses **eleven numbered vertices** because eleven is the smallest suitable prime for five distinct undirected chord families.

Each family advances by its own number of positions, called its **step** `k`:

| Attribute | Step `k` |
|---|---:|
| Rank | 1 |
| Tradition | 2 |
| Range | 3 |
| Duration | 4 |
| Primary Trait | 5 |

At every vertex `i` where an attribute's bit is `1`, that attribute adds a connection from `i` to:

$$
(i+k)\bmod 11
$$

Here `i` is the active vertex number, `k` is the attribute's step, and `mod 11` means **wrap around to vertex 0 after vertex 10**. A `0` bit adds no connection. A **chord** is this encoded, undirected pair of endpoints; it remains the same chord if the renderer later draws a curved rather than a straight line.

**Output of Layer 1:** five separate sets of encoded vertex-to-vertex connections, one set per primary attribute.

## 4. Layer 2 — Orbits

Adding four more chord families would increase the number of crossing connections. Instead, Layer 2 uses the shared eleven-bit words to calculate a **single orbit value at each vertex**, without introducing any new vertex-to-vertex connection.

At a given vertex, an active **Damage** bit contributes **1**, **Area** contributes **2**, **Casting time** contributes **4**, and **Casting traits** contributes **8**. An inactive bit contributes nothing. Add the contributions to obtain `U`, an integer from **0 through 15**. Because the weights are successive powers of two, every combination of active attributes has a different total; the four bits can be recovered from that total.

The number determines the amount of a circle to draw around that vertex:

$$
\text{orbit sweep} = U\times 24^\circ
$$

An orbit value of `0` draws nothing, while `15` gives a complete **360°** circle. Intermediate values give partial circular arcs. An **orbit is one combined arc or circle centered on that vertex**: it is neither four separate rings nor a curved chord between two vertices. The **sweep angle** is calculated information; the orbit's radius and decorative styling are drawing choices.

## 5. Layer 3 — Spell fingerprint

Two distinct spells can share all nine categorical mechanics, so their chords and orbits can be identical. To distinguish records independently of those mechanics, Layer 3 stores a **spell fingerprint** based on the assigned **source/variant ID**. It is **not** a tenth mechanical attribute, an encoding of the spell name, or a hash of the mechanical values.

The calculation forms the pair `['spell-id', variant]`, with the variant represented as a string, **serializes it as JSON**, and converts the JSON text into **UTF-8 bytes**. It then prepends a **16-bit header that records the number of JSON bytes**, followed by eight bits for each byte. The supplied calculation guide specifies a **192-byte limit for the complete JSON payload**, not merely the ID text.

These bits occupy ordered marker positions. Each `1` is visibly marked; each `0` still has a position but is left unmarked. Changing the marker shape or track layout does not change the spell fingerprint bits.

Different assigned IDs produce different fingerprints, including when the mechanical layers coincide. This is a **catalogue-record distinction, not a universal identity guarantee**: manually reused custom IDs or IDs reused across catalogues can still collide.

## 6. Drawing and filtering — after calculation

Only after the three layers are calculated does the renderer decide how to **show** them. It places the eleven logical vertices along a chosen contour, then draws Layer 1's endpoint pairs as straight or curved connections. Bending a chord does not change its encoded endpoints. It draws Layer 2's circular orbits **around their own vertices**; a curved Layer 1 chord must not be confused with an orbit. Finally, it places Layer 3's fingerprint bits in ordered marker slots. Marker style and placement affect appearance, not the underlying sequence.

A deterministic **rank-based visibility filter** makes lower-rank sigils *look* less crowded. It always retains the **Rank-family chords**. Other Layer 1 chords and **whole Layer 2 orbits** form the optional pool; the renderer retains a rank-dependent fraction of that pool in a stable order, rounding the number shown upward. It never truncates an orbit's sweep to achieve the percentage.

| Rank | Optional mechanical elements displayed |
|---|---:|
| Cantrip | 20% |
| 1–3 | 40% |
| 4–6 | 60% |
| 7–8 | 80% |
| 9–10 | 100% |

These percentages **do not apply** to Rank-family chords, the spell fingerprint, or every visible part of the drawing. The rule uses Rank as a *display heuristic*; it does not claim that every lower-rank spell has intrinsically simpler mechanics. Hiding a stroke or an entire orbit **does not recalculate the spell, delete its encoded data, or alter its fingerprint**.

## 7. One compact worked example

This **constructed example** illustrates the calculation; it is **not a published Pathfinder 2e spell**. The following JSON uses the editor's attribute IDs: `effectTrait` is Primary Trait, `castActions` is Casting time, `castTraits` is Casting traits, and `variant` is the source/variant ID.

```{.json #worked-example}
{
  "rank": "cantrip",
  "tradition": "Arcane",
  "range": "Self",
  "duration": "Instant",
  "effectTrait": "Healing",
  "damage": "Acid",
  "area": "none",
  "castActions": "1 action",
  "castTraits": "none",
  "variant": "demo-1"
}
```

The calculation audit reads this input and the results table below directly from
this guide, then checks them against the application calculation and option lists.
Arrays list one result per vertex or orbit, in vertex order.

<!-- worked-example-results -->
| Property | Result |
|---|---|
| Non-none bits | `"00001111000"` |
| None bits | `"00000000000"` |
| Active vertices | `[4, 5, 6, 7]` |
| Rank chords | `4` |
| Other chords | `16` |
| Orbits | `4` |
| Orbit units | `[5, 5, 5, 5]` |
| Orbit sweeps (degrees) | `[120, 120, 120, 120]` |
| Fingerprint payload bytes | `21` |
| Fingerprint bits | `184` |
| Optional elements | `20` |
| Optional elements shown | `4` |
| Visible mechanical elements | `8` |
| Total mechanical elements | `24` |
<!-- /worked-example-results -->

**Shared bits and Vertices:** every non-`none` value is the first meaningful
option in its attribute list, so each uses the same rotated word. All four
active vertices produce a connection for each primary attribute. The Rank
connections are **4 to 5, 5 to 6, 6 to 7, and 7 to 8**, not just the first pair.

**Orbits:** at each active vertex, Damage contributes weight 1 and Casting time
contributes weight 4. Area and Casting traits encode zero bits and contribute
nothing. Thus each orbit has `U = 1 + 4 = 5`, and its sweep is
`5 * 24 = 120` degrees. These are four partial orbits, not complete circles.
All four active attribute bits at the same vertex would instead yield
`U = 15` and a complete 360-degree circle.

**Spell fingerprint:** the JSON payload `["spell-id","demo-1"]` is encoded as UTF-8
and prefixed with its 16-bit byte length. The resulting bit count describes
ordered marker positions, not necessarily visible marks.

**Rank filter:** a cantrip shows 20% of the optional pool (other connections and
whole orbits), rounded upward, plus every Rank connection. Hidden elements and
fingerprint bits remain unchanged.

The complete internal mechanical encoding can be reconstructed when the same option lists and necklace dictionary are available, and the complete fingerprint bits retain the assigned ID. A **filtered drawing, screenshot, or exported image is not guaranteed to be losslessly decodable**: some calculated strokes may be absent, and visible geometry alone need not preserve every bit.

## 8. Sources and scope

- [*The Spell Writing Guide*](https://www.gorillaofdestiny.com/books-and-compendiums), by The Gorilla of Destiny: conceptual foundation for binary-pattern and chord-based spell writing. **Vertex-centered orbits, the spell fingerprint, and rank-based visibility filtering are Sigil extensions**, not rules attributed to that Guide.
- `ATTRIBUTE-OPTIMIZATION.md`: the historical analysis named in the revision instructions. Its **1,403-record** scope and the **seven-required / nine-maximum** constraints are taken from that brief; the underlying analysis file was **not supplied** for independent inspection.
- `HOW-IT-IS-CALCULATED(1).qmd`: the supplied baseline for the **current** eleven-vertex, five-chord/four-orbit calculation, fingerprint format, filtering behavior, and stated **1,400-record** catalogue size.

The current implementation is in `src/spell-calculation.ts`, `src/spell-encoding.ts`,
`src/spell-drawing.ts`, and `src/constants.ts`. The calculation audit checks the
worked example above against those calculation and option definitions, alongside
independent checks of all sixteen orbit masks, necklace ordering, fingerprint
encoding, and rank filtering. Run it with `npm run test:math`. These checks do
not rerun or validate the historical attribute-selection experiment.
